title: Batching heuristics shadow-run observations
content:
Summary:

This doc captures notes from the shadow run we executed to evaluate the new batching heuristics (adaptive-window + priority bucketing) against production traffic shape. The run focused on assessing throughput uplift, p99/p999 latency behavior, and stability under mixed short/long sequence workloads. Results were surprising: steady-state throughput improved ~12% for model-v2-8b-ff16, but we observed intermittent microbursts causing p999 spikes and some request stalls around cold-prefix transitions.

What we ran (quick config):
- window_algorithm: adaptive-window-v2 (min_batch_ms=3, max_batch_ms=22)
- priority: prefetched-prefix-priority enabled for requests with kv_cache_hits >= 1
- model: model-v2-8b-ff16 (quantized int8 profile)
- nodes: 8 x A100-80GB (dedicated test cluster), serving-runtime commit: 5f2b9a3
- traffic: shadowed production qps ~ 420 (mixture: 65% short <128, 25% mid 128-512, 10% long >512)
- duration: 4 hours (2026-03-12 02:00-06:00 UTC)

Key metrics (comparison: baseline heuristics -> adaptive-window-v2):
- aggregate token throughput: +12.3%
- median latency (per-token generation): -4% (improved)
- p95: -2%
- p99: +8% (worse)
- p999: +35% (spikes, intermittent)
- error rate: unchanged (~0.03%)

Observed behaviors and traces: 
- Microburst pattern: p999 spikes correlate with short bursts of long-sequence requests that arrive shortly after a period dominated by short-sequence traffic. Visual traces show a 50-300ms cluster of elevated service time on a subset of GPUs.
- Cold-prefix stalls: several stalled requests (~200-400ms extra) that align with new priority-bucketing when a prefetched prefix was misclassified (kv_cache metadata missing for ~0.8% of requests). Those requests fell into a lower-priority queue then got re-prioritized causing queue reshuffling and a temporary scheduling backlog.
- Lock contention: flame graphs and mutex histograms show elevated lock hold times in batch_scheduler::enqueue_routing (approx +2.1x median hold time vs baseline) during spike windows. Hypothesis: when bucket boundaries shift, more frequent queue merges cause the scheduler to serialize updates.
- Uneven GPU skew: a small subset (1-2) of worker shards showed consistently higher tail latencies; investigation shows those machines had slightly older kernel versions and a different memcpy path that made small-batch throughput weaker.

Reproduction notes and quick checks: 
1) Re-ran a 30m targeted test with synthetic traffic that mimics production short->long sequence transitions at scale factor 1.2 and reproduced p999 spikes within 7 minutes.
2) Disabled priority re-bucketing while keeping adaptive-window: p999 spikes reduced but did not disappear (suggests both heuristics interact).
3) Isolated queue merge code path by stubbing re-prioritization: with stubs we removed the queue reshuffle, and observed lock hold time drop and p999 back to baseline.

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1 (primary): Frequent bucket boundary shifts plus re-prioritization logic cause serialized queue merges that increase scheduler lock contention, producing microburst-induced p999 spikes.
- H2: A small percentage of worker nodes with out-of-date kernel/libcaffe/memcpy behave worse on small-batch loads, amplifying tail when spikes route to those shards.
- H3: KV cache metadata race leads to misclassification of prefetched prefixes, causing unexpected queue moves and extra latency for individual requests.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Anton Li: instrument batch_scheduler to emit per-bucket operation counts and lock hold percentiles (task: add metrics and an opt-in verbose trace flag) — due 2026-03-16.
- Gabriela Ortiz: schedule a kernel/libc version audit and collect sysinfo from worker shards that showed skew (task: run sysinfo probe across test cluster) — due 2026-03-15.
- Samir Patel: create a temporary guard in priority bucketing that adds a "no-op debounce" (ignore bucket boundary changes < 500ms) and run a 2-hour shadow to validate effect — due 2026-03-17.
- Priya (me): triage the misclassified kv_cache cases and add a lightweight assertion in the metadata write path to catch races in debug builds — due 2026-03-18.

Decisions from the sync: 
- Do not roll adaptive-window-v2 to production yet. Need two validation runs: (a) priority debounce enabled, (b) nodes normalized (kernel parity) and lock metrics observed.
- Short-term mitigation: enable per-shard routing isolation to limit how many concurrent long-seq requests can be sent to a single shard in a 5s window (config knob, conservative default).

Notes for follow-ups/longer-term: 
- Consider reworking re-prioritization to an eventual-consistency model: rather than in-place queue merges, use append-only small staging queues per-bucket with a background shuttler to minimize scheduler locks. This adds complexity but could decouple hot path.
- Explore hybrid priority that is probabilistic rather than deterministic on kv_cache_hits to reduce boundary-churn.
- Add a service-level test to our CI that replays short->long traffic transitions and validates p999 under a threshold; run nightly in the perf cluster.

Meeting attendees and quick log: 
- Present: Priya Raman (notes), Anton Li, Gabriela Ortiz, Samir Patel, Maya Chen (SRE), John Duarte (runtime), Danica Reyes (product-ops).
- Key callouts: Maya suggested adding a coordinator-level guard to prevent rapid reassignments; John flagged the memcpy difference on older kernels as likely multiplier.

Appendix: example trace ids and snippets (for follow-ups)
- trace: run-2026-03-12-03:14:12 id=a1b2c3d4 sample: p999 spike event aligned with queue-merge op @ batch_scheduler.cpp:442
- trace: run-2026-03-12-05:01:33 id=f6e7d8c9 sample: cold-prefix misclass -> re-prioritize -> 320ms stall

Next sync: 2026-03-17 15:00 UTC (perf sync) — bring instrumented metrics and initial debounce shadow run results.
